wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.name: Lake outlet climbers' path into the west cirque
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles with a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek near the 1.5-mile mark, then left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, a second log crossing, and steep rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about four miles and 2,280 ft, an hour and three quarters to two hours for a fit party carrying a rack.

The shorter of the two ways into the west cirque starts at the lake outlet, at the north end below the small dam. Cross there and follow a well-cairned climbers' path across the timbered hillside; it gains height quickly and deposits you on the talus field under the west face. Reckon about an hour from the lake, plus twenty to twenty-five minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the wall itself.

This is the way parties who have been there recommend, and it is the one to take unless the outlet crossing is unreasonable.

Colchuck Lake is the last water. The cirque and the route are dry.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.season: mid-Jul-Sep, once the gully and cirque talus are snow-free
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges can be slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
The outlet crossing below the dam is a real crossing, not a step-across
Cirque talus is loose and the boulder-hop to the wall is ankle-breaking ground
Snow can linger in the approach terrain into early summer
No water above Colchuck Lake
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.baseFinding:
You are looking for the start of the West Face route on a wall that carries half a dozen hard lines, so the useful information is what sits either side of it.

The West Face route's first pitch begins at a left-facing, lightly vegetated corner at the base of the wall. That corner is the thing to find. From the talus you scramble up to a ledge and the first pitch goes from there.

Orient yourself with the neighbours: The Tempest starts lower than the West Face and lies to its right, taking a system of cracks up a black-streaked headwall — the black streaking is visible from the talus and is a good negative marker. The Scoop is further right again, right of both the West Face and the Tempest. Scarface climbs the large, obvious pale rock scar on the formation, several hundred feet right of the old northwest buttress line. If you are under black streaks or under a conspicuous scar, you are right of where you want to be.

Rack up on the talus rather than at the wall — the base is boulders and the flat ground is below.

wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.name: Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.notes:
The alternative when you do not want to cross the outlet. Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, then cut north through a band of slide alder — look for cairns, because this is a genuine bushwhack — and climb the leftmost gully about 1,000 ft to its top. From there contour east on easy ground into the cirque.

An hour and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line and a lot more brush, but no ford. A winter/spring variation on the same idea follows a steepening gully starting near the lake's southwest edge.

In a heavy year the gully holds snow well into early summer and an axe or light traction is worth having.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the gully holds snow into early summer
hazards: Slide alder band is a real bushwhack; cairns are the only guide
1,000 ft of loose gully
Lingering snow in the gully into early summer
More elevation gain than the outlet approach
No water above Colchuck Lake
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.baseFinding:
Once you contour east into the cirque, the base identification is the same as the outlet approach: find the left-facing, lightly vegetated corner at the foot of the wall, and use the black-streaked headwall of The Tempest and the pale rock scar of Scarface, both to the right, to confirm you have not drifted along the base.

The difference this way in is that you arrive in the cirque from the south, higher up, so your first sight of the wall is from the side rather than head-on. Walk out into the talus and look at the face square-on before committing to a start; foreshortened from the flank, several corners look like the corner.

wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.name: Colchuck Lake, snow-covered glacier (early season)
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.notes:
Stuart Lake Trail #1599 from the FR 7601 road end for about 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.6 miles of steep switchbacks through boulders to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Call it four miles and 2,200 ft. This is the last reliable water.

Follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail. Gain the crest of the lateral moraine as early as you can — the alternative is a long session in genuinely loose scree and talus, and parties consistently report an hour of boulder-hopping through it when they stay low.

With good snow cover much of this basin, and later much of the glacier, can be glissaded on the way out, which is why parties favour the early window. Aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon: it softens badly and post-holing plus wet-slide potential make a late descent both slow and unpleasant.
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.season: Jun-early Jul, while the glacier is well filled and crevasses stay bridged
hazards: Loose scree and talus if you do not gain the moraine crest early
Rockfall off the surrounding faces onto the glacier, worst during the morning warm-up
Moats and thin bridging at the glacier margins
~100 ft of 40-degree snow below the col
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
Glissading the descent is normal here and is also how people get hurt — axe in hand, clear runout
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.baseFinding:
This route's 'base' is the toe of the glacier, at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft, and the way to know you are there is that the moraine crest you have been walking runs out against continuous snow that keeps rising ahead of you.

From the toe, take the left (east) lobe of the glacier. That side passes directly beneath the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone routes — seeing that big northwest wall on your left is the confirmation you are on the correct lobe. You are climbing beside those routes, not on them.

The glacier is easy angle for most of its length and then steepens for the last stretch: about 100 ft of 40-degree snow immediately below the Colchuck-Dragontail col (Colchuck Col / Banshee Pass) at roughly 8,200 ft. If the angle has not kicked back, you are not at the col yet.

From the col the summit is northwest: 3rd-class sandy steps up to a summit plateau around 8,500 ft, then continue west and north over the plateau to the true summit at 8,705 ft. The plateau is the trap in cloud — it is broad and flat and the first high ground you reach on it is not the summit.

wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.name: Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late season)
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.notes:
The walk to Colchuck Lake and up the moraine is the same, and easier without snow. What changes is everything above the moraine.

By August the glacier typically melts out to hard, sun-cupped ice. It is not heavily crevassed, but crevasses and marginal moats that were bridged in June are open, and the surface no longer takes a boot step. Crampons and an axe stop being optional and a rope becomes a real consideration for the margins.

The scree and talus below the moraine is at its loosest now, and rockfall off the surrounding walls is more frequent with no snow holding things in place. The glissade descent is gone — plan on down-climbing everything you came up, which is the main reason the day gets longer.
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.season: Aug-Sep, once the glacier has opened up and gone to bare, sun-cupped ice
hazards: Bare sun-cupped ice: crampons and axe required, self-arrest unreliable
Open crevasses and moats at the glacier margins
Increased rockfall from the surrounding faces with no snow cover
No glissade descent — the day is longer at both ends
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.baseFinding:
The same landmarks, read differently. The toe of the glacier is further up the basin than it was in June — glacial retreat and seasonal melt both push it back — so the moraine crest walk is longer before you meet ice.

Stay on the left (east) lobe under the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone routes. Late in the season a thin crevasse zone has been reported opening on the descent side, and parties are advised to stay climber's left of it coming down.

The steepening to about 40 degrees immediately below the Colchuck-Dragontail col at roughly 8,200 ft is still the marker that you have arrived, and on bare ice it feels considerably more serious than the same slope in snow.

wa_concord_tower_north_face.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
wa_concord_tower_north_face.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route walk-in, which is why the two are so often climbed on the same day. Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass; about 1.75 miles of maintained trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream, marked with a large cairn; then the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the bowl below the towers and up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft.

In the gully, staying climber's left for the lower two thirds and then crossing to climber's right keeps you on the most stable ground.
hazards: loose, heavily trafficked gully below the notch — helmets, and don't queue underneath another party
hollow-sounding flakes on the upper pitches send debris to the notch
no water above the stream at the Trail #727 junction
wa_concord_tower_north_face.baseFinding: The route starts AT the top of the notch, on the Concord (south) side — not below it. Stand on the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord col and turn to face Concord Tower: the first pitch is the crack system running up that wall to a large ledge holding a few small trees, and that ledge is the pitch-one belay and is visible from the notch. The mistake to avoid is dropping 30 feet down the Liberty Bell side to the tree with the ledge running left into a blocky chimney — that is the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell, the other tower, and parties heading for opposite summits share this saddle all day. If your first pitch tops out on a treed ledge you are on Concord; if it starts by walking a small ledge leftward into a chimney you are on Liberty Bell.

wa_concord_tower_north_face.name: Early-season snow to the notch
wa_concord_tower_north_face.notes:
Same line, but the gully feeding the Liberty Bell-Concord notch holds snow into late June most years and the boot path lower down may still be buried. Ice axe standard, crampons if it has refrozen.

One upside of the early season here: while the gully is snow-filled the rock in it is locked in place, and rockfall gets noticeably worse once it melts out.

SR-20 is closed across Washington Pass every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so this window begins whenever the highway reopens.
hazards: firm snow in the gully with a long runout below
moat between snow and rock at the base
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access until the highway reopens
wa_concord_tower_north_face.baseFinding: Snow does not move the start — it is still the crack system on the Concord wall rising directly from the crest of the notch to the treed ledge. What snow does is fill the notch, so the col reads as a smooth saddle and the base of the first pitch can sit above a moat. Look up at the tower on the south side of the col for the treed ledge to confirm you are on the right wall before committing.

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large tailings pile around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its west side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
hazards: No drivable trailhead; ferry and shuttle logistics, closed by a recent flood and landslide
Creek crossings run high in early season; one depends on a footbridge that may be out
Standing dead timber and loose footing on the steep burned hillside above the tailings
Several notches in the spur ridge, most Class 5 from below; picking the wrong one is the crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the diminished glacier, worst late summer
Loose Class 3-4 gully to the notch and a short exposed Class 4 step below the summit ridge
Very remote, no cell service, multi-day self-rescue
wa_copper_peak_south_route.baseFinding: The arrival test is a notch, and it is the best negative marker on this peak: several notches cut the spur ridge and most of them are class 5 from below. The one you want is the highest notch you can reach easily, gained by a loose Class 3-4 gully on climber's right — the north side — near the top of the glacier. Picking it is the route. If the notch in front of you needs fifth-class moves to enter, it is the wrong notch and there is a better one further up and right. How you know you are under it: you have crossed the glacier remnant on the east face, roped, and you are near its top. The glacier is a fraction of its mapped size and crevasses are usually minor and walkable around, but the moats along the rock margins are what show themselves late in the summer. The stream is the handrail from camp: leave the trail at the bench, ford to the west side, and follow the outlet stream that drains the glacier. It comes from the thing you are walking to, so in cloud it is a line you can follow uphill without seeing anything. What happens immediately after the notch, so you can confirm you took the right one: turn left and traverse a short, steep snowfield — roughly a hundred feet of exposed side-hilling that usually wants crampons and is worth a belay if the surface has gone hard. Once on the crest, blocky Class 3 leads up the ridge to the summit. Notch, then a hundred feet of side-hill snow, then the crest. If there is no snow traverse beyond the notch, you are in a different one. The last obstacle is one move, not a pitch. A single short, exposed Class 3+ or 4 step sits just below the top, and some parties carry a short handline for one airy notch there — a fixed handline, not a rappel. If you are looking for rappel anchors on this route you will not find any; nothing on it is rappelled. A note on the route's name: the south-east in this route's aspect is the glacier remnant itself, which faces south-east from under the spur ridge on the peak's east side; the finish is on the upper north-east ridge. Navigate by the glacier and the notch, not by the compass point in the name.

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: From the Phelps Creek trailhead, walk up through Spider Meadow and the Spider Glacier to Spider Gap, drop past the Lyman Glacier to Lyman Lake, then follow the Railroad Creek trail down the valley to Copper Creek. It avoids the boat and shuttle but is far longer, with a steep snow climb to the gap.
hazards: Far longer approach with a steep snow climb to Spider Gap
Descent past Lyman Glacier, then a long valley walk to Copper Creek
Burned hillside with standing dead timber and loose footing on the Copper Creek trail
Several notches in the spur ridge, most Class 5 from below; picking the wrong one is the crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the glacier remnant, worst late summer
Loose Class 3-4 gully and a short exposed Class 4 step; very remote, no cell service

wa_crater_mountain_standard_route.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
wa_crater_mountain_standard_route.notes: Park at the Canyon Creek trailhead at about 1,900 ft on Highway 20 near milepost 141, roughly fifty-five miles west of Winthrop or thirty-three east of Marblemount. Vault toilet, no drinking water. There is no bridge over Canyon Creek on Jackita Ridge trail #738, and the Forest Service describes the crossing as difficult and potentially hazardous in spring and early summer. How people get across changes from year to year — one season a shin-deep wade a hundred yards upstream, another a log fifty metres up — so do not plan on a fixed method. The first mile and a half is brushy. The trail then climbs steeply through timber on a long series of switchbacks to the junction with the Crater Lake trail #746. That junction is unsigned, reported by two separate parties, and its elevation is published as either 5,000 or 5,260 ft. Turn onto #746 and climb toward Crater Lake. There is a second unmarked junction just before the lake, leading to the old east lookout site; stay with the main path, which runs along the south shore. Crater Lake is the last water — the ground above is dry, and the lake itself is shallow enough that water filtered at the outlet comes out warm. The whole peak is commonly given as fourteen to fifteen miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain.
wa_crater_mountain_standard_route.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; the Canyon Creek ford is the constraint in spring and early summer
hazards: An unbridged Canyon Creek ford, hazardous in spring and early summer, with no fixed crossing point
Yellow paint marks that lead into a steep, loose gully rather than along the better line
Loose rock through the scramble section, reported by most parties
No water above Crater Lake
Broken glass and nails around the old lookout remains on the east peak
wa_crater_mountain_standard_route.baseFinding: There are three markers above the lake and they come in order. First, at about 6,800 ft the grade mellows and the trail turns north. Two parties record the same elevation for it. Second, at about 7,600 ft the trail ends — it does not fade, it disappears into a loose gully, and three accounts agree on the height. That is where the scrambling starts. Third, and this is the thing you can see: the gully is marked by a downscoping ribbon of white rock and the first of several yellow painted X marks. One climber calls it pretty hard to miss once you know to look for it. Negative marker, and it is important because the marking itself is the trap: the paint tempts you straight up that gully. It starts well and turns steep and loose with rolling pebbles higher up. A party who followed the paint up found on the way down that the better line traverses across the gully and around the corner, where cairns lead upward. Once you reach a yellow arrow, the ground improves markedly for the rest of the way. How you know you have finished the hard part, corroborated four ways and genuinely reassuring: the scrambling ends well below the summit and real trail resumes. A mellow path runs the last quarter mile to the top, past the remnants of an old tramway at the top of the cliff section. If you are still scrambling within sight of the summit, you are off the line. There is one false top, a bump on the south ridge, and the trail bypasses it to the west — the real summit sits directly behind it and is not visible from below. Two things to have straight before you go, because both are commonly stated wrongly. The historic lookout stood on the highest summit, not a lower one; the second, lower lookout site is on a peak about a mile east. And the lookout tender here was Gary Snyder in 1952 — Jack Kerouac was on Desolation Peak, a different mountain some fifteen miles away, four years later. The summit register itself carries a card that conflates the two.

wa_crater_mountain_standard_route.name: Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
wa_crater_mountain_standard_route.notes:
A genuinely different approach with a specific purpose: it exists to avoid the Canyon Creek ford. The party who wrote it up said so directly, having judged a day trip from Canyon Creek to involve a difficult crossing at the time they were there.

It starts from the East Bank trailhead near Ruby Creek and runs roughly forty-eight miles with about 13,100 ft of gain over three days, taking in Devils Dome. That is a very different undertaking from the day-trip standard, and it is chosen for access rather than for the mountain.

Nothing is published on a Granite Creek or East Creek approach, so do not assume one exists.
wa_crater_mountain_standard_route.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, as a multi-day trip
hazards: A three-day committing loop with substantial cumulative gain
Same loose gully and misleading paint above
Long stretches with no bail-out
wa_crater_mountain_standard_route.baseFinding:
The summit end of the day is the same regardless of how you got into the basin: the trail dies around 7,600 ft into a loose gully marked by a ribbon of white rock and a yellow X, the paint leads you up rather than across, and the scrambling finishes well below the top where real trail resumes for the last quarter mile.

What differs is your bearing on arrival. Coming round by Devils Dome you meet the peak from the north-east rather than up from Crater Lake, so identify the south-ridge false top and the white ribbon from a distance before dropping into the basin, rather than expecting to walk into them off a known trail.

wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier and through West Challenger Notch
camps: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.notes:
From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, the Hannegan Pass Trail runs about 4 miles and 2,500 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River valley and loses most of the gain again.

The valley traverse passes Copper Creek Camp around mile 9 and U.S. Cabin Camp around mile 12; expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin and, in blowdown years, real timber. One party logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks beyond the cable-car crossing. The Chilliwack is crossed on a hand-pulled cable car, which is mandatory and somewhat exposed; the river is not reliably fordable.

Beyond it the Brush Creek Trail climbs to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, roughly 17 miles in. From Whatcom Camp, leave trail and traverse below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank on the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass, about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft. Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From there rope up, climb the Challenger Glacier to a high bench near 8,100 ft, and descend through West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Round trip is on the order of 40 miles.
wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.season: Jun-Sep. The Crooked Thumb Glacier itself can be severely crevassed with open moats late in the season
hazards: Mandatory hand-pulled cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack River; river not reliably fordable
Blowdown on the Chilliwack River trail, about two hours per 1.5 miles in bad years
Crevasses and open moats on the Whatcom, Challenger and Crooked Thumb Glaciers
40-45 degree snow couloir that wants pickets or flukes when firm
Loose Class 4-5 rock on the upper route; weathered fixed tat on the horn
Exposed 5.8+/A1 summit headwall; extreme remoteness, multi-day self-rescue
wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.baseFinding:
The route starts at the foot of a snow couloir on the northwest side, and the couloir is the only thing on the peak you can identify in cloud. From the moraine camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, the line goes up a 40-45 degree northwest-facing snow couloir to the saddle just north of the peak. In fog, do not navigate by the summit; navigate by the fact that you are in a confined snow gully with rock walls on both sides, steepening steadily to about 45 degrees. If the ground opens out and flattens, you are on the glacier, not in the couloir.

Arrival at camp, which is the harder find: the camp is a lateral moraine, i.e. a ridge of rubble sitting on the ice, reached by descending through West Challenger Notch off the Challenger Glacier bench at about 8,100 ft. The notch is the crux of the navigation, not the couloir. You are through it when the ground stops dropping and you are standing on loose rock with ice on both sides.

Confirm on the climb: above the couloir the route works along loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles, and the crux is a single roughly 10 ft near-vertical crack, 5.8+ or 5.2 with a point of aid, taken at the top of a headwall. A rock horn draped with old slings sits below those pinnacles. If you have climbed the couloir and are on clean, moderate rock with good stances, you are not on this route; everything here is described as horribly loose.

What going too far looks like: continuing up the Challenger Glacier past the 8,100 ft bench instead of dropping through the notch takes you toward Challenger's own summit rocks, which is a different peak.

wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.name: Big Beaver valley and Wiley Ridge

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier lateral moraine
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the base for the climb itself, on the narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the glacier after crossing the high bench near 8,100 ft and dropping through the West Challenger notch. Fully exposed alpine ground with no shelter and long views out to the volcanoes. The moraine is loose and the glacier below it is heavily crevassed with big moats late in the season — rope up leaving camp, not after.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: tight — a narrow strip, enough for a small party

bivy.name: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
bivy.notes: Emergency ledge, not a camp — a small stair-stepped shelf on the descent ridge overlooking the precipitous east face, where a party spent an unplanned full night out. No water, no shelter, cold, and highly exposed. On a peak this far in, a benightment is a realistic outcome rather than a remote one, so it is worth knowing this ledge is there and worth carrying enough to survive it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp

wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.notes: Take the water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing and follow the Big Beaver trail up the valley toward Luna Camp. Leave the trail and climb Wiley Ridge off-trail to the basin on its south side, then continue to the Challenger Arm and cross to West Challenger Notch above the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Expect several days and serious bushwhacking.
hazards: Water taxi, then serious bushwhacking up Wiley Ridge off-trail over several days
Crossing the Challenger Arm to West Challenger Notch above the glacier
Crevasses and big moats on the Crooked Thumb Glacier late in the season; loose moraine camp
40-45 degree snow couloir that wants pickets or flukes when firm
Loose Class 4-5 rock on the upper route; weathered fixed tat
Exposed summit headwall; extreme remoteness, multi-day self-rescue

wa_dark_peak_dark_glacier_route.name: Swamp Creek climbers' path to the col
wa_dark_peak_dark_glacier_route.notes: This is the line most descriptions still call standard, and it is the brushy one. From the road end at the bridge, follow the crest trail south to the first creekside camp and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork. Leave the maintained trail there for the long-abandoned climbers' path: cross Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and force about a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple. Above that a headwall bars the basin; the way up it is at the far left, and the route then climbs steep forest, veering right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Beyond lies a further, higher basin near 5,500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier.
wa_dark_peak_dark_glacier_route.season: Early to mid summer gives firm, well-bridged snow with least crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are open and the glacier is less stable.
hazards: About a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple on an officially abandoned path
A forested cut up the headwall to the right of the waterfall looks like the way and is not — taking it forces a Class 3/4 rock wall in the trees
The slab cut onto the glacier is easy snow early in the season and a gully with a stream running in it later, needing Class 2/3 slab work
The glacier is genuinely crevassed; roped travel with crevasse rescue capability is the expectation
Wet-loose runouts come off snow slabs perched on wet rock along the glacier margins
The moat crossing onto the summit rock varies through the season and can be the hardest move of the climb late in a dry year
wa_dark_peak_dark_glacier_route.baseFinding: The headwall has a tempting wrong line on it, and the glacier has a tempting wrong line above it. Coming up the basin the headwall looks formidable; the way up is at its far left, through a brushy gully where the headwall corners, and there is an appetising forested cut up the wall to the right of the waterfall that must not be taken — cutting right early forces you onto the low end of the rock wall in the trees. Above, steep forest veers right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft, where a piece of orange flagging has marked the way. Beyond that, a third and higher basin near 5,500 ft sits below the slabs of the receding glacier, and a natural cut on that basin's southwest side leads through the slabs onto the ice: easy snow early in the season, later a gully with a stream in it. Once on the glacier, the second trap: a snow and talus slope under the north side of the summit looks enticing and leads to the northeast ridge, which is far more exposed and saves nothing. Do not take it.

wa_dark_peak_dark_glacier_route.name: Crest trail to Hemlock Camp and the northwest climb
wa_dark_peak_dark_glacier_route.notes: The newer variant continues farther south on the crest trail, roughly to the Hemlock camp, then leaves the trail and climbs northwest through open forest and slopes — about 3,500 ft of gain — to reach the glacier from the ridge above. It avoids nearly all of the Swamp Creek brush and is substantially easier ground, even though the Swamp Creek line is still the one usually called standard. It is the better choice for a party that wants to arrive with something left, and it is what the far side of the ridge separating this peak from its neighbour gives access to.
wa_dark_peak_dark_glacier_route.season: Early to mid summer for the best glacier conditions, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
hazards: Trackless climbing through open forest and slopes with no established line
The drop-in onto the glacier off the ridge has needed a rappel
Crevasses, and the season-dependent moat crossing onto the summit rock
The gentle-looking snowfield on the north side of the summit ridge ends in a dead vertical rock face
Many unbalanced rocks on the final crest, and cornices along it early in the season
wa_dark_peak_dark_glacier_route.baseFinding: Open forest and slopes, not brush, is the sign you are on this variant. Leaving the crest trail farther south, the climb northwest gains roughly 3,500 ft through timber and open slope that stays walkable; if you are fighting slide alder and vine maple you have started up the Swamp Creek drainage instead and are on the older, much harder line. Veer left near the top of the drainage to reach the drop-in point onto the glacier — parties have needed a rappel to get off the ridge here, so carry the means to do it. Once on the ice, ignore the snow and talus slope running up under the north side of the summit: it looks enticing from the glacier and leads to the northeast ridge, which is much more exposed and saves no time. Leave the glacier by crossing the moat onto the rock instead, then take the three step-ups — up and left, up and left, up and left — to gain the west spur around 8,200 ft, east of the actual saddle.

wa_direct_north_buttress.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
camps: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
wa_direct_north_buttress.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
wa_direct_north_buttress.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: Chilliwack River crossing in high water; cable car or ford
Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
Steep brushy timber, slide alder and a loose divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir below the wall
Deep moat at the toe of the buttress late season
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Remote and committing, several days from help
wa_direct_north_buttress.baseFinding:
The Direct starts at the very bottom of the rock, and that is what separates it from the route it shares a camp with. From the saddle you first go down: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

The toe of the buttress lies on the right-hand side of that ice, where the rock runs down into the snow. That junction is the start. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

The negative marker is unambiguous and it is the common mistake: the regular North Buttress walks past this toe and continues up the glacier on the buttress's climber's-left side, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. If you are still walking on snow with the buttress rising to your right, you have walked past the Direct and are heading for the regular start. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A second check is how soon it gets hard. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

Watch the moat at the junction. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

wa_direct_north_buttress.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. The alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is shorter, but the cross-border stretch can be heavy bushwhacking, so the long trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

approachLogistics.trailhead: Chilliwack Lake road, south end (British Columbia)

wa_direct_north_buttress.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
wa_direct_north_buttress.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: International border crossing on foot
Overgrown, unmaintained tread; heavy bushwhacking on the cross-border stretch
Same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall below the buttress
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Cross-border rescue complications; remote and committing
wa_direct_north_buttress.baseFinding:
Arrival differs, the start does not. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

Tie in at the toe of the rock on the right-hand side of the ice, where the buttress runs down into the snow and there is no more snow above you. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
hazards: Brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log; trail destroyed by an old avalanche swath near 4,500 ft
Open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Dome Glacier
Narrow, exposed rock arete near the summit; many parties belay or rappel part of it
Cairned cross-country traverse to the glacier is easy to lose in cloud
Cornices on the upper ridge; remote, multi-day approach
wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.baseFinding:
From Itswoot Ridge the traverse north-east toward the Dome Glacier goes through a basin that is well marked with cairns and is followable even with reduced visibility — so in cloud, look for cairns rather than trying to hold a bearing. Losing the cairns is the sign you have drifted.

The climbing starts where you rope up at the glacier's edge. The upper Dome Glacier is mellow, so the arrival is undramatic; the feature you are climbing to is the notch or col at 8,560 ft immediately north of the summit block. It is confirmed by what happens on the far side: from the col a snow slope of about three hundred feet and then a rock arete of about five hundred feet lead to the summit at 8,920 ft.

The useful cross-check in poor visibility is that the col also gives onto the Chickamin Glacier beyond — a much larger icefield than the one you came up. So a very big glacier appearing on the far side is correct and not a sign you are in the wrong place; the thing to verify is that the summit block is immediately to your south. If the ground on the far side does not drop away onto a large icefield, you are at a different notch.

wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass

bivy.name: Dome-Dana col
bivy.notes: A high perch around 7,300 ft used by parties who want to shorten summit day or who are linking the Ptarmigan Traverse. It puts you above the traverse and its route-finding, with the upper Dome Glacier — which parties describe as mellow — immediately above. The trade is no running water and full exposure; the ridge camp lower down is the more common choice, and pushing this high is generally judged not to save enough time to be worth it.
bivy.permit: No permit or quota in Glacier Peak Wilderness
bivy.capacity: Small; two parties have camped there at once

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road)

wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
hazards: Multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
Crevasses on the Dome Glacier and a bergschrund below the notch
Narrow, exposed rock arete near the summit; many parties belay or rappel part of it
Cornices on the upper ridge
Remote terrain, long evacuation if injured
Camp at the Dome-Dana col has snowmelt water only
wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.baseFinding: Arriving from the north along the traverse, the reference points are the same: the cairned basin traverse toward the Dome Glacier, and the 8,560 ft col north of the summit block with the Chickamin Glacier beyond it and the summit rock arete immediately to the south.

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
camps: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: From the road-end trailhead start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed beside Beverly Creek, and at the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the wrong valley for this peak. The Bean Creek tread climbs through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley, drops to a ford of Bean Creek, then keeps climbing until the forest breaks open into a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. That basin is the last dependable water. At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than left into the upper basin; tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking to a broad saddle on the divide.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.season: Class 2 on dry ground from July into October, and a popular spring snow climb before that, when an axe and sometimes crampons are wanted on the steep south-facing summit slopes.
hazards: Bean Creek ford runs cold and pushy in May and June
Old avalanche debris crosses the trail just above the ford
Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge that is easy to kick onto a party below
No dependable water above the meadows
Steep, icy south-facing snow on spring ascents
Afternoon heat on the exposed ridge
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.baseFinding: At the saddle, straight on goes somewhere else and the peak is left and straight up. Above the flower basin the tread goes intermittent through upper meadows and switchbacks to a broad, largely treeless saddle on the divide between the two drainages, around 6,200 ft, with scattered flat tent sites on it. The climbers' track up the peak is obvious underfoot but carries no marker of any kind — no cairn, no post, no blazed tree — so the test is the fork rather than a landmark: carrying straight on to the east takes you toward the far creek and away from the mountain, while the summit line turns left, to the north, and goes straight up the ridge. If you are still among flower meadow and old-growth stands you are in the basin below and have not reached the saddle at all. The upper ridge is roughly 800 vertical feet of unrelenting loose scree, sand and broken rock with the track fading in and out. Accounts disagree about whether there is one false top or several undulating bumps below the summit, so treat any high point with more ridge rising beyond it as another bump rather than the end.

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Standup Creek trail

bivy.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
bivy.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. The state ownership is the thing to internalise: the boundary between Community Forest rules and national forest rules falls partway up this road, camping law changes at it, and the change is not signed as clearly as it should be. Above the boundary the gravel road washboards badly by August, holds snow into early summer, and was subject to closure orders following the 2025 fire.
bivy.water: No potable water. Bring what you need or filter from the Teanaway River, which runs beside all three and is dependable year round at this elevation — a useful contrast with everything higher in the valley, which is snowmelt-fed and unreliable after July.
bivy.permit: This is state Community Forest land, not national forest, and the rules are genuinely different from the Forest Service ground further up the road. The campgrounds are free but a Discover Pass is required to park. Dispersed camping is prohibited anywhere in the Community Forest — camping is confined to these designated campgrounds, and this is actively enforced, so the roadside pullout habit that works on the national forest above does not work down here. Stays are capped at seven days in any thirty. Rubbish is not collected, so everything packs out, and cutting firewood is not permitted. Fire restrictions arrive early and are strict.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley: roughly fifty-nine sites at 29 Pines, about fifty-five at the Teanaway camping area, and eleven plus two group sites at Indian Camp. All first come, first served, no reservations. Equestrian camping is confined to Indian Camp and the Teanaway camping area.

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: From the Standup Creek trailhead, the trail runs up a gentle valley, then steepens through open hillside to the southwest ridge of Earl Peak, where a boot path leads to the summit. Quieter and gentler at first than the Bean Creek side, with the hard climbing saved for the upper slopes.
hazards: Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge that is easy to kick onto a party below
Steep, icy south-facing snow on spring ascents
Afternoon heat on the exposed ridge
Boot path on the upper southwest ridge; descent on loose sandy scree is more error-prone

wa_east_face.name: Downey Creek, Bachelor Creek and Itswoot Ridge
camps: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_east_face.notes: From the Suiattle River Road, follow the Downey Creek trail up the valley, then turn up Bachelor Creek on a faint, brushy path toward Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge. From the ridge, cross the glaciers east toward the Gunsight Range. Plan on a long two-day approach.
hazards: Long multi-day glaciated approach with route-finding and brushy bushwhacking
Crevasse fields on the Chickamin Glacier approach and descent
Bergschrund or moat at the route base may need boulder-hopping or a bypass
Exposed alpine climbing on the east face with significant fall consequence
Afternoon rockfall on the south-facing rappel descent
Rapid weather changes in exposed positions
Remote, self-rescue-only terrain

wa_east_face.name: From Stehekin up Agnes and Spruce Creeks
wa_east_face.notes: From High Bridge on the Stehekin Valley Road, follow the Pacific Crest Trail south up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence, crossing both creeks on logs. Then go cross-country, through dense brush, up toward the Icy-Spruce col for a high camp facing the Gunsights. Reaching Stehekin takes a boat or floatplane, so this is a multi-day trip.
hazards: Roughly ten miles up Agnes Creek with two log creek crossings
Dense brush on the cross-country climb toward the Icy-Spruce col
Reaching Stehekin needs a boat or floatplane, so the trip is multi-day and committing
Bergschrund or moat at the route base may need boulder-hopping or a bypass
Exposed alpine climbing on the east face with significant fall consequence
Afternoon rockfall on the south-facing rappel descent
Remote, self-rescue-only terrain

wa_east_ridge_2.name: The Kindy Creek roadbed and the ribbon-marked climbers' trail to the Point 5116 saddle
wa_east_ridge_2.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles to the signed forest road 1570 junction and turn right. Cross the river on a concrete bridge and continue about half a mile to a Y-junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders; park there, at roughly 1,150 to 1,300 ft, because a long-standing washout keeps most parties from driving higher.

A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every fifty to a hundred and fifty feet leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth - about seventeen hundred vertical feet in its first mile, with few switchbacks - to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. From the saddle the route climbs roughly a thousand feet to Peak 5791, then traverses heather benches and meadows above the lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of the east ridge.
hazards: a rooty, eroded and very slick steep mile that is worse descending than ascending
an easy-to-miss junction at the saddle where the two routes on this peak diverge
no water on the steep climb from the roadbed
rolling ridge travel that takes longer than the distance suggests
an exposed camp and no bail-out once out on the ridge
wa_east_ridge_2.baseFinding:
The junction at the saddle is the whole point of this approach and it is easy to miss. At the ridge saddle near Point 5116, go left and climb about a thousand feet to Peak 5791.

The pink ribbon is the handrail on the steep mile below. It is spaced closely enough that losing sight of it for long means you have drifted; the tread is rooty and eroded and very slick when wet, so on the descent the ribbon matters more than the ground does.

Above the saddle the markers are two named high points in order: Peak 5791 first, then heather benches and meadows above the lake, then Peak 5860 crossed or contoured. You should pass two distinct points before the ridge begins - arriving at what you take for the base without having crossed them means you are short.

The base itself is where the east ridge rises out of the ground above the lake basin and runs west toward the summit. If the ground ahead of you is a glacier rather than a ridge, you have contoured past the ridge's foot and joined the standard route's approach to the ice. The east ridge is rock and heather with air on both sides; the standard route crosses snow.

wa_east_ridge_2.name: Camping at the lake below the ridge
wa_east_ridge_2.notes: The lake below the ridge is the common overnight for this route and turns it from a very long day into a comfortable two. The camping is in the meadows on the lake's east side and there is reliable water. Parties doing it in a day still pass through the same ground and should treat the lake as the last water before the ridge.
hazards: no water above the lake
a wind-exposed basin camp
loose blocks where the ridge rises out of the benches
committing ridge travel with no easy descent off either side
wa_east_ridge_2.baseFinding:
From the lake the base of the east ridge is gained by crossing or contouring Peak 5860 and continuing on heather benches above the basin. The ridge foot is where that benched ground runs out against the crest and the rock begins rising west toward the summit.

The test is that you are on a crest, not on a bench. Once established the ground should fall away on both sides. Heather benches with a wall above you and the basin below are still the approach.

And the negative marker is snow. If you are stepping onto glacier ice, you have contoured round past the foot of the ridge and are on the standard route's ground. Turn back and gain the crest.

Carry water from the lake. There is none on the ridge.
